text: In the 1960s nobody knew if the Moon was solid ground or deep, fluffy dust that would swallow a spacecraft. NASA had to find out before sending astronauts. On April 17, 1967, an Atlas-Centaur rocket launched me from Cape Kennedy to get the answer.
I did not stop in orbit. My Centaur stage aimed me directly at the Moon, and for about 65 hours I coasted through space, folded up and quiet, with one small course correction along the way.

Radar measured my height while my rocket engines slowed me down. Reflections off bright rocks confused the radar, so my engines did not shut off in time. I bounced twice before settling into a small crater in the Ocean of Storms.
I carried a scoop on an arm, a first for the Moon. Controllers on Earth used it to dig trenches, squeeze the soil and drop it. My TV camera sent back 6,315 pictures of my new home.
The soil behaved like damp sand: soft on top, firmer underneath. Strong enough to hold a spacecraft, and strong enough to hold astronauts. The way was clear for Apollo.

In November 1969, Apollo 12 landed about 180 meters away. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over and cut off my camera to carry home, so engineers could study what 31 months on the Moon does to metal, glass and wires.

I still stand in my crater, missing a few parts. My brothers Surveyor 1, 5, 6 and 7 are out there too. Surveyor 6 even made the first lift-off from the Moon, a short hop of a few meters. We were the scouts. Apollo followed.
July 16, 1969. I was folded inside the Saturn V, the most powerful rocket that had ever flown. Above me sat the command module Columbia, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins.
After leaving Earth orbit, Columbia turned around, docked with me and pulled me free of the rocket. Together we coasted for three days across 384,000 km of space.
On July 20, Armstrong and Aldrin floated into me. We undocked from Columbia, Collins stayed in orbit, and I fired my descent engine to begin falling toward the Sea of Tranquility.

The computer flashed alarms and the planned spot was full of boulders. Armstrong took manual control, flew me over the rocks, and touched down with fuel running very low. Then came the words: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.
Six and a half hours later, Armstrong climbed down my ladder and stepped onto the Moon. The two astronauts collected rocks, set up experiments and planted a flag, all within sight of me.
After 21 and a half hours on the surface, the astronauts climbed into my top half, the ascent stage. It fired its own engine and lifted off, using me as its launch pad. I stayed behind.
Near me the crew left a laser retroreflector. Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at it today. The timing shows the Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, about 3.8 centimeters every year.

Apollo 11's rocks gave the first clues that the young Moon was covered by an ocean of molten rock. Samples from later missions showed the Moon is about 4.5 billion years old. Five more crews landed after us.
I still stand in the Sea of Tranquility. A plaque on my leg reads: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.

November 14, 1969. I was packed inside the Lunar Module of Apollo 12. Just after liftoff our Saturn V was struck by lightning, twice! Power alarms lit up, but a quick fix from the ground and the crew saved the mission.
Apollo 12 had a special target: land right next to an old robot, Surveyor 3, which had been sitting on the Moon for two and a half years.
Pete Conrad and Alan Bean steered their Lunar Module, Intrepid, down just 180 meters from Surveyor 3. It proved astronauts could land exactly where they planned.
Astronauts could only stay a short time. So they set me up: instruments wired to a central station with a radio, powered by a small nuclear generator that turned heat into electricity.

My seismometer could feel tiny vibrations. When the crew crashed their used ascent stage into the Moon on purpose, I felt the Moon ring like a bell for almost an hour. Over eight years our network recorded thousands of moonquakes.
Quake waves bend and slow down as they pass through different layers. Our data showed the Moon has a crust, a mantle and a small core, like Earth, but it is cold and quiet inside.

On September 30, 1977, NASA switched all five stations off to save money. We are silent now. But the laser mirrors left at Apollo 11, 14 and 15 need no power, and observatories still aim lasers at them today.
July 26, 1971. Apollo 15 launched on a Saturn V, with me folded flat against the side of the Lunar Module Falcon. I was the first car ever sent to another world.
Four days later Dave Scott and Jim Irwin flew Falcon down between the Apennine Mountains and a winding canyon called Hadley Rille, the most daring landing site of Apollo so far.
I was stored folded in half with my wheels tucked in. The astronauts pulled on straps and I unfolded, swung down and dropped to the ground, ready to roll.
Rubber tires would fail in the Moon's extreme heat and cold, so my wheels were woven from zinc-coated piano wire with titanium treads. Each wheel had its own electric motor, powered by two batteries.

Walking in spacesuits is tiring. With me, crews could drive kilometers away to mountains and canyon edges. On the slopes of Mount Hadley Delta the crew found the Genesis Rock, a piece of the Moon's ancient crust.
Apollo 16 and 17 brought rovers too. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt drove about 36 km on Apollo 17. Rovers let astronauts reach far more places and bring back far more kinds of rock.

At the end of each mission the crew parked the rover a short distance away and pointed its TV camera at the lander, so people on Earth could watch the lift-off live. Three of us are still parked on the Moon.

August 20, 1975. A Titan IIIE-Centaur launched me from Cape Canaveral. I was really two spacecraft: an orbiter, and me, the lander, sealed inside a protective shell. Viking 2 followed three weeks later.
Our curving path around the Sun took ten months. I had been heat-sterilized before launch so no Earth germs could fool my search for life on Mars.
We reached Mars orbit in June 1976. The planned landing site looked too rough in orbiter photos, so scientists searched for weeks. My landing date slipped from July 4 to July 20.

I separated from the orbiter and plunged into the thin Martian air inside my heat shield. A parachute opened, then three engines with 18 small nozzles each fired, spreading their blast so they would not disturb the soil I came to study.
I touched down seven years to the day after Apollo 11. Within minutes I sent back the first photo ever taken on the surface of Mars: my own footpad on rocky ground.
My robotic arm scooped soil into a tiny automated biology lab. My instruments fed it nutrients to see if anything living would breathe out gas.
Some tests reacted, but other instruments found no organic material. Most scientists decided strange soil chemistry, not life, caused the reactions. The debate inspired every Mars mission since.
I reported Martian weather for over six years while my orbiter mapped the whole planet. Viking taught NASA how to land on Mars, and set the plan for later missions: follow the water.
In November 1982 a faulty command pointed my antenna away from Earth, and we never spoke again. My twin went quiet in 1980. We both still stand exactly where we touched down.

December 4, 1996. A Delta II launched Mars Pathfinder, a mission meant to prove NASA could reach Mars quickly and cheaply. Tucked on one of the lander's petals was me, a rover the size of a microwave oven.
We flew for seven months. Unlike Viking, Pathfinder did not stop in orbit first. It flew straight into the Martian atmosphere at about 26,000 km/h.
A heat shield took the fire. A parachute opened. Then, seconds before impact, giant airbags inflated around the lander like a bunch of grapes and small rockets fired to slow us down.
We hit the ground and bounced about 15 times, some bounces as high as a building, before rolling to a stop. Then the airbags deflated, the petals opened, and Mars was all around us.
I drove down a ramp onto the dirt. I weighed 10.6 kg and moved about 1 centimeter per second, and my six wheels used a rocker-bogie suspension that let me climb over rocks.

Scientists named the rocks around me: Barnacle Bill, Yogi, Scooby-Doo. My APXS instrument read their chemistry. Many looked rounded and stacked by water, a sign that huge floods once rushed through this valley.
My rocker-bogie wheels and Pathfinder's airbag landing were reused. Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance all roll on the same idea I tested first.

My lander relayed my messages home. When it went silent on September 27, 1997, I could no longer talk to Earth. My mission was planned for 7 days. I lasted 83. I am parked near the lander, now named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
June 10, 2003. A Delta II launched me from Cape Canaveral. My twin Opportunity followed a month later. We were robot geologists, sent to find out if water once flowed on Mars.
Mars and Earth are never that far apart in a straight line, but spacecraft must curve around the Sun. My path stretched about 487 million km over seven months.
I hit the atmosphere at about 19,300 km/h. Heat shield, parachute, rockets, then airbags, all in about six minutes, with no help from Earth. The radio signal took ten minutes to reach home.
I bounced to a stop in Gusev Crater, a giant crater scientists thought once held a lake. I rolled off my lander with cameras, a rock grinder and tools to read the chemistry of stones.
The plains around me were mostly volcanic rock. So I drove over 2 km to the Columbia Hills and climbed all the way to the top of Husband Hill. A rover climbing a mountain on Mars!
In 2006 my right front wheel stopped turning. So I drove backward, dragging it. That turned out to be lucky: the dragging wheel scraped up bright white soil that was almost pure silica.
Silica like that forms in hot springs or steam vents. On Earth such places are full of microbes. My discoveries at Home Plate showed Mars once had spots that might have been habitable.
In 2009 I broke through a crust into soft sand at a place called Troy and could not get out. I could not tilt my solar panels toward the winter Sun. My last message came March 22, 2010.
July 7, 2003. A Delta II Heavy launched me one month after my twin Spirit. I was headed for Meridiani Planum, where orbiters had spotted hematite, a mineral that often forms in water.
Spirit landed three weeks before me. While I flew, I listened to the news: my twin was safe on the other side of Mars.
Heat shield, parachute, retrorockets, airbags. Same recipe as Spirit, aimed at a smooth plain halfway around the planet.
I bounced and rolled straight into a small crater, Eagle crater. Right in front of me was layered bedrock, exactly what scientists had dreamed of. They called it an interplanetary hole in one.
The ground was covered in tiny gray balls nicknamed blueberries. They are hematite, which forms in water. Together with the layered rocks, they proved liquid water once soaked this place.
Engineers hoped I would drive about 600 meters. I kept going for years, to Victoria crater and then giant Endeavour crater. In 2015 I passed a full marathon distance, the first ever on another world.
My discoveries helped convince scientists that ancient Mars had liquid water at its surface. That shaped where Curiosity and Perseverance were sent to search for signs of past life.

In June 2018 a dust storm covered the whole planet and blocked out the Sun. My solar panels could not make power. After more than 1,000 attempts to wake me, the team said goodbye in February 2019. I rest in Perseverance Valley.

August 4, 2007. A Delta II launched me from Cape Canaveral. My name comes from a bird that rises from ashes: I was built from a lander cancelled years earlier and lessons learned from one that was lost.
For ten months I flew toward the far north of Mars, where the Mars Odyssey orbiter had detected lots of hydrogen just under the ground. Hydrogen there usually means ice.

I fell through the atmosphere inside my heat shield and opened my parachute. High above, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter snapped a photo of me hanging under it, the first picture of a spacecraft landing on another world.
I landed on three legs using pulsing rocket engines, the first to do so on Mars since Viking. Around me: polygon-shaped cracks everywhere, like frozen ground in Earth's arctic.
My robotic arm dug trenches. Bright white chunks appeared, and days later they had vanished, turning straight into vapor. Only ice does that. My oven then heated a sample and confirmed it: water.
My laser saw snow falling from clouds, turning to vapor before it reached the ground. I also found perchlorate salts in the soil, which help water stay liquid in the cold.
Finding shallow ice changed how scientists picture Mars today, and where future astronauts might find water to drink or turn into rocket fuel.
I was built for one Martian summer. When winter came the Sun stayed down, and I went silent on November 2, 2008. Orbiter photos later showed heavy ice had broken my solar panels.
May 5, 2018. An Atlas V lifted me off from Vandenberg in California. Two briefcase-sized satellites called MarCO came along, the first tiny CubeSats ever sent to another planet.
For six and a half months I traveled about 485 million km. The MarCO twins flew behind me, ready to relay my landing signal home.
I hit the atmosphere at about 19,800 km/h. In under seven minutes, heat shield, parachute and twelve descent engines slowed me to walking speed.
Other missions studied the surface. I came to study the inside. I landed on a flat, boring plain, chosen on purpose: flat, quiet ground is best for listening.

My arm set my seismometer on the ground under a dome to block the wind. It was so sensitive it could detect motions smaller than an atom. I recorded 1,319 marsquakes, including a big magnitude 5 in 2022.
Quake waves change as they pass through different layers. By timing them, scientists measured Mars' crust and mantle and found its liquid metal core is bigger than expected.
That first map of the inside of another rocky planet helps explain how planets like Earth formed and cooled. I even felt meteorites smash into Mars.
Dust slowly covered my round solar panels until December 2022, when I sent my last message. My final words to Earth: Don't worry about me, my time here has been both productive and serene.
July 30, 2020. An Atlas V launched the Perseverance rover from Cape Canaveral. Folded under its belly was me: a 1.8 kg helicopter, an experiment that might not work at all.
We traveled about 470 million km. Along the way the rover topped up my batteries and checked that I was healthy.
Our spacecraft plunged into the Martian air. A supersonic parachute opened, and the rover's computer compared camera images with maps to pick a safe spot by itself.
A rocket-powered sky crane hovered above the floor of Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed, and lowered Perseverance on cables. Then it cut the cords and flew off to crash far away.
The rover lowered me to the ground and drove away so my solar panel could see the Sun. I had to survive my first freezing night alone, at about minus 90 degrees Celsius.

Air on Mars is about 1 percent as thick as Earth's, so my rotors spin about 2,400 times a minute. I rose 3 meters, hovered and landed. A scrap of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer rides under my solar panel.
I was planned for 5 test flights in 30 days. I made 72 flights over almost 3 years, scouting routes and photographing places ahead of Perseverance. Future Mars missions now plan to bring helicopters.

On my 72nd flight, over smooth featureless sand, my rotor blades were damaged during landing. I can never fly again. I stand on a sand ripple in Jezero, a monument to the first flight on another world.
March 2, 1972. An Atlas-Centaur with an extra kick stage launched me so fast that I crossed the Moon's orbit just 11 hours later. Nothing had ever left Earth faster.
Some scientists feared the asteroid belt would be too crowded to cross. I flew straight through it, unharmed, and opened the road for every outer-planet explorer after me.
I became the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter. Its radiation was far stronger than expected and nearly fried my electronics, but I sent home the first close-up pictures of the giant planet.
Bolted to me is a gold-coated plaque showing a man and a woman, a map of our Sun's position using pulsars, and a drawing of our solar system with my path. A greeting, in case anyone ever finds me.
Because of us, Voyager 1 and 2 knew they could cross the asteroid belt and survive Jupiter's radiation. My twin Pioneer 11 used Jupiter's gravity to swing on to Saturn in 1979, the first visit there.
My nuclear power slowly faded. Earth heard my last faint signal on January 23, 2003. I am drifting toward the star Aldebaran and will pass it in about 2 million years.
February 17, 1996. A Delta II launched me from Cape Canaveral. I was the first mission of NASA's Discovery Program: smaller, faster, cheaper. My target was asteroid 433 Eros.
In June 1997 I flew past asteroid Mathilde, a dark rock so light it must be full of holes. Then I swung back past Earth for a gravity boost toward Eros.

In December 1998 my engine shut down early during the burn to enter orbit and I flew right past Eros. The team regrouped, and on Valentine's Day 2000 I became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid.
For a year I circled Eros, a potato-shaped rock about 34 km long, measuring its shape, gravity and chemistry. It is one solid, ancient piece of the early solar system covered in boulders and dust.
I was never built to land. But the team tried a slow descent anyway, and I touched down at about 6 km/h. I still worked! My gamma-ray sensor read the ground for two more weeks.
What I learned helped plan later missions that touched asteroids and brought samples home, like Japan's Hayabusa and NASA's OSIRIS-REx.
My last contact was February 28, 2001. I still sit on Eros, riding along as it loops around the Sun, sometimes passing closer to Earth than Mars ever does.
September 27, 2007. A Delta II Heavy launched me on a mission no spacecraft had tried: orbit one world beyond Earth, leave it, and orbit another.

My ion engines push with the force of a sheet of paper resting on your hand. Tiny, but they can run for years. In 2009 I swung past Mars for a boost. Over time that gentle push added up to more speed change than any spacecraft before me.

I arrived at giant asteroid Vesta and found a huge crater at its south pole with a central peak about 22 km high, more than twice as tall as Mount Everest. Many meteorites found on Earth were blasted from that impact.
Then I left Vesta and spiraled to dwarf planet Ceres. I spotted dazzling bright spots in Occator crater. They are salt deposits left by salty water seeping up from below.
Vesta and Ceres are leftovers from when planets formed. Studying both showed how water and heat shaped baby planets, and that Ceres may still hide salty liquid deep inside.

I ran out of the fuel that pointed my antenna and fell silent on November 1, 2018. I was left in a high orbit so I would not crash into Ceres for decades, keeping its surface clean for future explorers.
March 6, 2009. A Delta II launched me into the night sky from Cape Canaveral. I carried the biggest camera NASA had sent to space at the time, built from 42 light sensors.
Instead of circling Earth, I followed it around the Sun, slowly drifting behind. Far from Earth's glare, I could stare at the same stars without interruption.
I watched about 150,000 stars at once. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims a tiny bit. Watch the light curve: that little dip is a planet.
Before me, we knew a few hundred planets around other stars. I found more than 2,600. Most stars have planets, and many may have Earth-sized worlds where liquid water could exist.
In 2013 two of my four reaction wheels failed and I could not point steadily. Engineers balanced me using the gentle pressure of sunlight. My second life, called K2, kept finding planets for years.
Thanks to my data we now think there are more planets than stars in our galaxy. TESS and the James Webb Space Telescope now study the worlds I helped find.
I ran out of fuel and was retired on October 30, 2018. I orbit the Sun, slowly falling behind Earth. Scientists are still finding new planets in my data.
